newsitem.title: UK: London Stock Exchange risks row over new trading rules.
newsitem.headline: London Stock Exchange risks row over new trading rules.

text.p: The London Stock Exchange set out on Friday to pare controversial privileges that allow market-makers to keep big share trades secret.
The Exchange proposed to remove rules that allow delays to the publication of large trades, risking a fresh dispute with London's financial community.
In the latest chapter in a long-running debate about reforming the London market, the Exchange said it aimed to make the workings of the market more open and transparent.
But some brokers said such privileges are important because they allow multi-million share trades to be carried out without market rivals manipulating prices to undercut their deals.

Market experts warned that activity in the market could be curtailed if the Exchange held to too strict a line on the disclosure of large share trades, pointing out that in globalised electronic markets deals could move away from the London Stock Exchange.
"If every you try to shackle the London market with this sort of regulation you will bury us because the business will move offshore," said the head of equity trading at one leading investment bank.

"You will never get institutions to reveal their intent, which is what they seem to be trying to do," the head of equity trading said. "You have to allow the market to work itself out, there has to be a balance between immediacy of reporting and risk-taking."
The Exchange said that financial services consultants Oliver, Wyman and Co had recommended immediate publication for all trades on execution.
It said the consultants had suggested that large or "block" trades be disclosed after 90 percent of the trade was executed, or at the end of the day.
The Exchange said it would explore whether trades could be published at a lower threshold, after 70 percent was executed, without adversely affecting liquidity.

With the Exchange under pressure to ensure transparent markets from Britain's financial industry regulators and an influential Parliamentary committee, which has been monitoring its reform plans, some said change was inevitable.
"It's a sign of the times, everyone is asking for more transparency," said Jim Rowley, former operations director at SBC Warburg and now chairman of a specialist brokerage in emerging markets.
Some were positive on the Exchange's latest proposals.

"This is an important statement as to how the market will work," said a senior executive at another leading broker. "It is a good compromise all round that should satisfy the regulators and the Treasury Committee and that will mean we will still be able to price risk competitively."
Yet it spells further change for the structure of firms trading shares in Europe's busiest stock market. "It's one more nail in the coffin for the market-makers," said Rowley.
The role of market-makers is set to change this year when the Exchange moves into an electronic share trading regime.
The planned order-driven system will match buyers and sellers of shares electronically.
Under the exchange's current quote-driven system, prices are set by market-makers. It is the only major exchange that still employs such a system.
The Exchange is still thrashing out the rules for its electronic order-driven system. The new proposals are now being discussed with the Securities and Investments Board, the Exchange said.
Eliminating the publication delay is sharp departure from the exchange's previous position, as it had argued in the past that doing away with the rule would compromise market liquidity.
Details of the new rules are still to be settled yet traders said a more transparent system was inevitable.

"There will be a lot of people complaining about any change of system but I think we have no option but to change because that is what the Exchange wants and the regulators want," said one industry executive.
